value.overview: The Cinnamon Hummingbird (Amazilia rutila) is a medium-sized hummingbird of dry and seasonally dry lowlands from western Mexico through Central America to Costa Rica. It is named for its warm cinnamon-colored underparts and rufous tail. This active nectar feeder is also an important pollinator of flowering plants. In Costa Rica, it is especially associated with the northern Pacific lowlands, where dry forest, open woodland, gardens, and flowering forest edges provide suitable conditions.
value.classification: The Cinnamon Hummingbird belongs to the hummingbird family Trochilidae and the order Apodiformes. It is one of the New World hummingbirds in the genus Amazilia.
value.identification: This hummingbird is about 9.5 to 10 centimeters long. The upperparts are green to bronze-green, while the underparts are a fairly uniform cinnamon or rufous color, with a somewhat paler throat. The tail is distinctly rufous, helping separate it from many other Costa Rican hummingbirds. The male usually has a red bill with a black tip. The female has more black on the upper bill, with red mainly near the base. Juveniles often show rufous edging on the head and back.
value.rangeHabitat: The Cinnamon Hummingbird ranges from the Pacific slope of western Mexico south through Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras, Nicaragua, and Costa Rica. In Costa Rica it is a resident species, most regular in the northern Pacific lowlands and foothills, including Guanacaste, and extending south to areas near Orotina and the Tárcoles River. It occurs from near sea level to about 500 meters, locally reaching around 1,000 meters west of the Central Valley. Preferred habitats include deciduous and semi-deciduous forest, older second growth, thorny scrub, savanna, gallery forest, forest edges, gardens, and other open areas with flowering plants.
value.migrationStatus: It is generally nonmigratory and resident in Costa Rica. Local movements may follow flowering and changing food availability, but it does not undertake a regular long-distance migration. It is only accidental or very uncommon on the Caribbean slope of Costa Rica.
value.breeding: In Costa Rica, breeding is reported mainly from December through May or June. The female builds a small cup-shaped nest from soft plant fibers and other fine materials, binding it with spider webs and often decorating the outside with lichens. The nest is usually placed 1 to 5 meters above the ground on a slender branch in a shrub, woodland edge, or forest understory. The female alone incubates the eggs and cares for the young, while the male defends feeding territories rather than assisting with nesting.
value.dietFeeding: The Cinnamon Hummingbird feeds primarily on nectar from a wide variety of flowering plants, especially flowers with tubular or otherwise accessible corollas. In Costa Rica it visits flowering plants in dry forest, gardens, and open woodland, including native species such as Passiflora vitifolia. It supplements nectar with small insects and other tiny arthropods, which provide protein and other nutrients. By moving pollen between flowers, it contributes to the reproduction of many tropical plants.
value.behavior: This species usually forages in the canopy, along forest edges, and around flowering shrubs and trees. It can hover while taking nectar and often makes repeated visits to productive flowers. Individuals defend feeding territories and may chase other hummingbirds or insects from favored flower patches. Its occurrence and local abundance can increase when major nectar sources bloom. Like other hummingbirds, it has rapid wingbeats and may become less active during cool or energy-poor periods.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is considered stable, although the total population size has not been reliably quantified.
